comments.why_zh: 关于高场磁体使紧凑型聚变成为可能的精彩演讲。
comments.quote_zh: 说真的，如果你喜欢这类东西，去看看这个演讲吧。很精彩。
comments.text_zh: 以我这个外行的理解，最近（大约过去 5 年）可用的、工业规模生产 rebco tape[1] 的工艺，正是超导技术中一项具体的进步，它特别使得用显著更小、更轻、更易管理的磁体获得更高的 tesla 磁场强度成为可能，于是你可以得到一个“足够强”的系统，能在小到可以由几所大学而不是几十个国家（也就是 ITER）来建造的规模上实现净正能量输出，因此这个工程项目的复杂度从“难以想象”降到了“只是非常高”。1 - [LINK] 2 - 几年前 MIT's Plasma Science Fusion Centre 一个关于此事的非常棒的演讲：[VIDEO]（说真的，如果你喜欢这类东西，去看看这个演讲吧。很精彩。）
comments.text: My layman's understanding is that recently available (~last 5 years) industrial scale processes to produce rebco tape[1] is the specific advance in superconductor tech that's specifically enabling higher tesla magnetic field strengths from significantly smaller and lighter and easier to manage magnets, so you can get a system that's "powerful enough" to run net posititve at a size that's small enough to be built by a few universities rather than a few dozen nations (i.e. ITER), so the complexity of the engineering project drops from "unimaginable" to "just very high". 1 - [LINK] 2 - really great talk from a few years ago about this from MIT's Plasma Science Fusion Centre: [VIDEO] (really, if you like this stuff, give the talk a watch. It's great.)

comments.text_zh: > 对聚变（等离子体）来说，规模就是一切。不。在聚变中，Q 才是一切。规模是托卡马克中提高 Q 的一种方式。通过增大规模来提高 Q 的问题在于，它会让反应堆变得不经济。像 ITER 这种尺寸的反应堆永远不可能在经济上可行，即使能够产生大量电力。幸运的是，扩大规模并不是提高 Q 的唯一方法。更好的方法是使用更强的磁场。用比我更有说服力的话来说：[VIDEO]
comments.text: > Scale is everything for fusion (plasma). No. Q is everything in fusion. Scale is one way to improve Q in a Tokamak. The problem with improving Q by increasing scale is that it makes the reactors uneconomical. A reactor the size of ITER cannot ever be economically viable, even was capable of producing massive amounts of electricity. Luckily, scaling up is not the only way to increase Q. The better way is to use more powerful magnetic fields. Put more eloquently than I can: [VIDEO]

comments.author: nharada
comments.story_title: ITER: World's largest nuclear fusion project begins assembly
comments.text_zh: 这里有一个很好的演讲，讲的是为什么 ITER 这么大：[VIDEO] 其核心思路基本上是：要想让托卡马克达到实现净能量所需的参数，要么需要非常强的磁体，要么需要一个很大的装置。在 ITER 设计的时候，他们用了当时能找到的最强磁体，然后把装置做得足够大，以达到想要的能量增益。这位演讲者认为，正是尺寸拖累了托卡马克的进展，因为它们变得太大，以至于建造它们成了一个庞大的多国项目。
comments.text: There's a good talk here about why ITER is so large: [VIDEO] The idea is essentially that to get the parameters needed to make net energy with tokamaks, you need either very strong magnets or a large device. At the time of ITER's design, they used the strongest magnets they could find and then made the thing big enough to get the energy gain they wanted. The speaker of this talk argues that it's size that stalled progress in tokamaks, since they'd become so big that building them became a massive, multinational project.

comments.author: MayeulC

comments.why_zh: 介绍聚变问题与现代方法。
comments.text_zh: 你的评论听起来像是你完全没理解其中的物理。铀跟这有什么关系？你说的“铀的性能”是什么意思？你觉得用“辐射”轰击它会发生什么？哪种“辐射”？铀最常用于裂变装置，而不是聚变装置。让铀发生聚变会吸收能量，而不是释放能量；这就是我们裂变它的原因。[LINK] 取暖的话，你不如用热泵。或者我想你可以拿些放射性材料并把它屏蔽起来。甚至用增殖反应堆，但那是裂变。我不想显得不尊重，但你说的东西听起来像炼金术，或者超级英雄电影里展示的那种“科学”。我能理解用一层金属产生 X 射线，并把这些射线聚焦来加热样品（顺便说一句，这有点像氢弹），但我也不是核物理学家。真正的物理学家比我们思考得多得多；如果存在通往实用聚变的简单路径，我们早就该知道了。我觉得你低估了这一切的复杂性（有点像 Dunning-Kruger 效应），去看看 “MIT's pathway to fusion[1]” 的视频，作为对这个问题和现代方法的入门 :) [1]: [VIDEO]
comments.text: Your comment makes it sound like you don't understand the physics of it at all. What does Uranium have to do with this? What does "performance of uranium" means? What do you think will happen when you bombard it with "radiation"? What kind of "radiation"? Uranium is most commonly used in fission devices, not fusion ones. Fusing Uranium would absorb energy, not liberate energy, this is why we split it. [LINK] For heating, you'd be better off using a heat pump. Or I guess you could take some radioactive material and shield it. Or even a breeder reactor, but that's fission. I do not want to come across as disrespectful, but what you're saying sounds like alchemy, or the kind of "science" they show in superhero movies. I could understand using a layer of metal to produce x-rays, and concentrate these to heat a sample (a bit similar to H-bombs, BTW), but I am not a nuclear physicist either. Real physicists have thought about this much more than we did, and if there was a simple pathway to practical fusion, we'd know about it by now. I think you underestimate the complexity of all this (kind of a "Dunning-Kruger" effect), go watch the "MIT's pathway to fusion[1]" videos for an introduction to the problem and modern approaches :) [1]: [VIDEO]
